clinicalPearls: DLB and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) are viewed as points along a single spectrum of Lewy body disease (LBD); LBD is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia after Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3491).

The timing between parkinsonism and dementia distinguishes the two: when dementia and neuropsychiatric symptoms precede or emerge alongside parkinsonism, the diagnosis is DLB; when dementia appears in a patient with long-standing PD, it is PDD (Harrison 22e p.3492).
Core diagnostic features of DLB are early psychosis with well-formed visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and parkinsonism (Harrison 22e p.3491).

The cognitive profile shows severe executive, attentional, and visuospatial deficits with relatively preserved episodic memory; prominent early episodic memory impairment instead suggests comorbid Alzheimer pathology (Harrison 22e p.3491-3492).
Fluctuations in attention and concentration can be marked, with short episodes of confusion or severe lethargy that may resolve rapidly (Harrison 22e p.3492).

Patients are highly sensitive to infectious and metabolic disturbances, and delirium precipitated by infection, a new medication, or systemic illness can be the first manifestation (Harrison 22e p.3492).

RBD, in which dream enactment occurs because normal dreaming muscle atonia is lost (sometimes causing injury to patient or bed partner), is a characteristic and often prodromal feature that may precede the syndrome by years (Harrison 22e p.3492).

A sense of a presence behind the person may precede well-formed hallucinations; delusions are less frequent and usually involve misidentification, infidelity, theft, or persecution (Harrison 22e p.3491-3492).
Autonomic and nonmotor features such as anosmia, constipation, depression, anxiety, orthostatic hypotension, and erectile dysfunction may appear early (Harrison 22e p.3492).
Incidence of DLB is roughly 7 per 100,000 person-years; prevalence of both DLB and PDD rises with age and both are more common in men (Harrison 22e p.3491).
About 10% of PD patients develop PDD per year, with most eventually progressing to dementia over time (Harrison 22e p.3491).
A profound cholinergic deficit from basal forebrain and pedunculopontine nucleus involvement underlies the fluctuations, inattention, and visual hallucinations (Harrison 22e p.3492).
harrison.pathophysiology: DLB is a synucleinopathy: the defining neuropathologic lesions are Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites distributed through specific brainstem nuclei, the substantia nigra, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, and ultimately the neocortex. Lewy bodies are intraneuronal cytoplasmic inclusions composed of straight 7-20 nm neurofilaments with surrounding amorphous material; they stain with PAS and ubiquitin and are now identified by antibodies to the presynaptic protein alpha-synuclein. Accumulation of alpha-synuclein aggregates in neurons and glia classifies DLB and PDD molecularly as synucleinopathies, though neuronal and synaptic loss (rather than Lewy pathology itself) best predicts clinical deficits. Pathology progresses through three stages: brainstem-predominant, transitional limbic, and diffuse neocortical. Disease is thought to propagate via a prion-like mechanism in which misfolded alpha-synuclein spreads transneuronally along connection pathways; PD often begins in the enteric nervous system and ascends via the vagus nerve, and/or in the olfactory bulb. A profound cholinergic deficit from basal forebrain and pedunculopontine nucleus loss drives fluctuations, inattention, and hallucinations, while locus coeruleus adrenergic deficits impair arousal and alerting. Both genetic and environmental factors contribute; alpha-synuclein gene duplications/triplications and GBA (glucocerebrosidase) mutations are linked to PDD/DLB presentations, supporting a double-hit hypothesis of toxins acting on a susceptible genetic background (Harrison 22e p.3492).
additionalDifferentials: Alzheimer's disease (and DLB with co-existing AD pathology)
Delirium from drugs, infection, or metabolic disturbance
nonInfectiousMimics: Multiple system atrophy, in which autonomic disturbance occurs earlier and is more severe and cognition is relatively preserved (anosmia favors LBD over MSA)
Alzheimer's disease, suggested by prominent early episodic memory and semantic naming impairment
Vascular parkinsonism or subdural hematoma identifiable on MRI
Drug-induced, infectious, or metabolic encephalopathy producing reversible cognitive change
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to exclude vascular parkinsonism or subdural hematoma and to look for the MSA 'hot-cross buns' pontine sign
Polysomnography demonstrating REM sleep behavior disorder without atonia
Seed amplification assays (e.g., RT-QuIC) detecting alpha-synuclein in CSF
Skin biopsy showing cutaneous alpha-synuclein deposition
I-123 MIBG cardiac scintigraphy showing postganglionic sympathetic denervation
Dopamine transporter imaging by SPECT or PET showing reduced striatal (particularly putaminal) dopamine transporter
FDG-PET showing occipital hypometabolism with relative posterior cingulate sparing (cingulate island sign)
CSF or blood phospho-tau217/phospho-tau181 when concurrent Alzheimer pathology is suspected
redFlags: New-onset delirium precipitated by infection, a new medicine, or systemic illness as the presenting feature
Severe sensitivity to dopaminergic medications and to typical neuroleptics, the latter risking neuroleptic malignant syndrome and death
Recurrent falls from early postural instability and orthostatic hypotension causing syncope
Violent dream enactment in RBD causing injury to patient or bed partner
harrison.prognosis: DLB is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with no currently available disease-modifying therapy; only symptomatic management exists. Severity of behavioral, sleep, and autonomic symptoms correlates with substantial caregiver burden, depression, and reduced caregiver quality of life (Harrison 22e p.3492-3493).
pitfalls: Misclassifying DLB as Alzheimer's disease because frequent AD co-pathology makes prediction of underlying disease challenging; prominent early episodic memory loss points to comorbid AD
Confusing DLB with MSA when autonomic features appear early; MSA autonomic dysfunction is earlier and more severe with relatively preserved cognition
Exposing patients to typical neuroleptics, anticholinergics, or dopamine agonists, which can trigger neuroleptic malignant syndrome or worsen symptoms
Overlooking that scattered Lewy body pathology in substantia nigra, amygdala, or olfactory bulb can be an incidental finding in healthy older individuals
Attributing fluctuating confusion solely to delirium and missing the underlying DLB diagnosis
harrison.severityClassification: Neuropathologic staging recognizes three stages of LBD progression: (1) brainstem-predominant, (2) transitional limbic, and (3) diffuse neocortical. Both DLB and PDD have a prodromal mild cognitive impairment (MCI) phase; prodromal MCI-Lewy body (MCI-LB) is distinguished from prodromal MCI-AD by clinical and biomarker features (Harrison 22e p.3492).
